clue.text: A form of security for wrongdoers

explanation.surface: A kind of protection designed with criminals in mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Stocks are shares held as financial securities; the stocks were also the wooden frame in which offenders were locked by the ankles for public punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Shares in a company are a form of financial security, and the old pillory-like frame held wrongdoers fast in the village square.

clue.text: So much gas from the Resident Magistrate

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A colonial magistrate is accused of being full of hot air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So much gas' is a quantity of gas: a therm is a unit of heat once used to bill British gas supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: A therm is a fixed unit of heat by which gas consumption used to be measured and charged.

clue.text: Hot food takes care of the doctor, as this does of his horse

definitions.text: as this does of his horse

parts.note: curry is a spicy, hot dish
a comb is what keeps the doctor's own hair tidy

explanation.surface: A doctor eats curry while grooming, just as a groom tends a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The comb looks after the doctor's hair as this tool looks after the horse's coat; the definition is the closing comparison.
explanation.definitionFit: A currycomb is a toothed grooming tool used to clean and dress a horse's coat.

clue.text: Fare that's a shilling higher

parts.note: s. was the abbreviation for a shilling in old British money
upper means higher up

explanation.surface: A meal that has gone up in price by a shilling.
explanation.walkthrough: A shilling was a pre-decimal British coin worth a twentieth of a pound, written s.
explanation.definitionFit: Fare is food, and an evening meal is one such serving of food.

clue.text: It might appear as a gross menace to sailors

indicators.note: the letters of the following words might appear in another order, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Something that looks like a huge danger to seafarers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might appear' turns AS A GROSS into the sea's name. The Sargasso Sea is a stretch of the Atlantic choked with seaweed, long feared by sailing ships as a place to be becalmed.
explanation.definitionFit: The weed-clogged Atlantic sea was long a hazard where sailing vessels could be trapped or becalmed.

clue.text: Proving the high quality of early films — or so they say

definitions.text: Proving the high quality of early films — or so they say

parts.words: Proving the high quality of early films — or so they say
parts.note: early films had no soundtrack, so the proverb praising quietness as precious is applied to them

explanation.surface: A claim that the first movies were of excellent quality.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent era of cinema is read through the proverb that holding one's tongue is worth more than speech; 'or so they say' marks a saying.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb holds that keeping quiet is more valuable than talking, and early films were wordless.

clue.text: Going over old ground to make new discoveries ?

definitions.text: Going over old ground to make new discoveries ?

parts.words: Going over old ground to make new discoveries ?
parts.note: the word split as a prefix meaning again plus looking for gives searching ground once more

explanation.surface: Retracing old steps in hope of finding something new.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as RE- (again) plus SEARCH: going over old ground. Read whole, it is the scholar's work of finding new things.
explanation.definitionFit: Systematic investigation aimed at discovering new facts is literally a seeking once more.

clue.text: Smith's Shoe Factory — scene of the strike

definitions.text: Smith's Shoe Factory — scene of the strike

parts.words: Smith's Shoe Factory — scene of the strike
parts.note: a blacksmith forges horseshoes on an iron block, hitting them with a hammer

explanation.surface: Industrial unrest breaks out at a firm making footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smith' is a blacksmith, not a company owner, and the 'strike' is a hammer blow, not a walkout; horseshoes are shaped on this block.
explanation.definitionFit: The blacksmith's heavy iron block is where horseshoes are hammered into shape.

clue.text: Dickensian Dick, of a mechanical turn

explanation.surface: A Dickens character with a bent for machinery.
explanation.walkthrough: Dick Swiveller is a character in Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop; read as a plain word it is a thing that swivels.
explanation.definitionFit: Dick Swiveller appears in The Old Curiosity Shop, and something that pivots on a mechanical joint can be called one that swivels.

clue.text: This was a capital film

parts.note: capital means both excellent and a chief city, and the 1927 Fritz Lang film is named for a great city

explanation.surface: Praise for a first-rate movie of the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' looks like old slang for excellent; it also means a chief city, the subject and title of Fritz Lang's 1927 silent film.
explanation.definitionFit: Fritz Lang's 1927 silent classic takes its title from the word for a great chief city.

clue.text: Latin poet's head is turned-there's nothing in it

indicators.note: the poet's opening letter is turned round so it comes after the next letter

parts.note: Ovid was a Roman poet; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: A Roman poet looks away, and his mind is empty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head is turned' swaps the first two letters of OVID, O and V, giving VO at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: An empty space or vacuum is a place with nothing inside.

clue.text: M.P. embraced by Jane comes to an exalted heaven

indicators.note: the politician is hugged within the heroine's surname

parts.note: Jane Eyre is Charlotte Brontë's heroine
MP is a Member of Parliament
taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician hugged by a woman named Jane finds himself in paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jane' is the Brontë heroine, known by her surname here; 'comes to' is a link meaning 'is followed by'.
explanation.definitionFit: In old cosmology the highest heaven, the realm of pure fire, bore this name.

clue.text: Like a lying dog !

parts.note: the proverb says to let sleeping dogs lie, so a lying dog is one that sleeps

explanation.surface: A remark comparing someone to a dishonest dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lying' suggests telling untruths; it means lying down, as in 'let sleeping dogs lie'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog lying down in the proverb is a sleeping one, dozing and unaware.

clue.text: What's the Saint got for Henry? Nothing

parts.note: Hal is a familiar form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal
O, the zero shape, means nothing

explanation.surface: A question about what a holy man has done for King Henry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link: HAL stands for Henry, and O follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Saints are traditionally painted with a ring of light round the head.

clue.text: Beware the awful ——" cried the Alpine peasant

definitions.text: Beware the awful ——" cried the Alpine peasant

parts.words: Beware the awful ——" cried the Alpine peasant
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from Longfellow's poem Excelsior, where an old man warns the climbing youth of snow

explanation.surface: A mountain villager shouts a warning to a traveller.
explanation.walkthrough: The line comes from Longfellow's Excelsior: 'Beware the pine-tree's withered branch! Beware the awful avalanche!'
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden mass of snow sliding down a mountainside is the danger an Alpine villager would warn of.

clue.text: Get round the honeydew consumer in triplicate

definitions.text: Get round the honeydew consumer in triplicate

parts.words: Get round the honeydew consumer in triplicate
parts.note: Coleridge's Kubla Khan says to weave a ring round him thrice, for he on honey-dew hath fed

explanation.surface: An instruction to surround someone who eats sweet stuff, three times over.
explanation.walkthrough: The allusion is to the end of Coleridge's Kubla Khan: 'Weave a circle round him thrice ... For he on honey-dew hath fed'.
explanation.definitionFit: To surround something is to form a ring about it, as Coleridge's onlookers are told to do.

clue.text: Imprisoned again a worker's sorry for his sins

parts.note: re- is a prefix meaning again
pent, as in pent up, means shut in
an ant is the crossword's worker insect; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: A labourer jailed for a second time regrets his wrongdoing.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who feels remorse for wrongdoing is contrite and penitent.

clue.text: What's the latest? Read news, maybe you will be

definitions.text: What's the latest? Read news, maybe you will be

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Someone asking for the latest is told to read the news to find out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges READ NEWS. Read as a whole, if you ask for the latest and read the news, your question has been met with a reply.
explanation.definitionFit: A question that gets a reply has been responded to, as reading the news would do for the asker.

clue.text: Worries about a container of firearms

indicators.note: the worries go round the outside of the container

parts.note: cares are worries
a bin is a container

explanation.surface: Anxieties surround a box holding guns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a container of firearms' looks like one phrase; 'of' is only a link to the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Carbines are short rifles, so they are a kind of gun.

clue.text: Plain needlework? Quite the reverse

parts.note: in knitting the plain stitch has an opposite, the inverted stitch

explanation.surface: Someone asks if the sewing is simple and is told the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' is a knitting stitch; the stitch that is its reverse is the one wanted, so 'Quite the reverse' defines rather than turns letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In knitting this inverted stitch is the opposite of a plain stitch.

clue.text: Odds returned ten to one on Musicmaker

parts.note: SP is the starting price, the odds at the off in horse racing
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: the number word is written backwards, as if sent back

explanation.surface: A bookmaker's ten-to-one-on bet comes back for a musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns TEN into NET. SP, the starting price, is a British racing term for a horse's odds.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinet is a small harpsichord, an instrument that makes music.

clue.text: Everyone needing outside pull to get fat

indicators.note: the word for everyone wants another word around it

parts.note: to tow is to pull
all means everyone

explanation.surface: Everybody needs to be pulled along to put on weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fat' looks like an adjective after 'get'; it is the noun, the animal fat used for candles.
explanation.definitionFit: Tallow is rendered animal fat used for candles and soap.

clue.text: Erica gets round in a foreign tongue

parts.note: Erica is the botanical genus of heaths, and ling is heather
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A woman named Erica travels around speaking another language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erica' looks like a woman's name; it is the heather genus, whose common plant ling gives LING.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingo is informal for a foreign language or jargon.

clue.text: Con man ?

parts.note: con is the against side of pros and cons, so a con man is one who argues against

explanation.surface: A swindler is under suspicion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Con man' looks like a fraudster; 'con' is the against side in 'pros and cons'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on the against side of a contest or argument is an adversary.

clue.text: 19'smother, we hear, from mother North area

parts.note: an acre is a unit of area

explanation.surface: A northern mother speaks of her home region.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 across is PURL, which sounds like pearl, so '19's mother, we hear' is mother-of-pearl; 'we hear' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nacre is the iridescent lining of shells, also called mother-of-pearl.

clue.text: "Presume not God to" (Pope)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from Pope's Essay on Man, where the line ends with a verb for examining closely

explanation.surface: A line of verse by Alexander Pope with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope's Essay on Man begins its second epistle: 'Know then thyself, presume not God to scan; The proper study of mankind is man.'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means scrutinise, so Pope warns against trying to examine the deity.

clue.text: do trop predicament of communist going to a French ball

parts.note: a communist is a red
un is French for a
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A communist feels out of place on going to a French ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'de trop' is French for too much or unwanted, so the predicament is being superfluous.
explanation.definitionFit: Being surplus to requirements is the state of superfluity, exactly what being de trop means.

clue.text: Obliged to see Ben beheaded

parts.note: to behold is to see

indicators.note: the name loses its first letter, its head

explanation.surface: A man feels he must watch Ben being executed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beheaded' removes B from BEN, leaving EN.
explanation.definitionFit: To be indebted or under obligation to someone is to be in their debt.

clue.text: Summer may go unsteadily be-before+ the fall

definitions.text: may go unsteadily be-before+ the fall

explanation.surface: Late summer days stagger towards autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summer' is not the season but one who sums, who tots up figures; and before a fall one may wobble on one's feet. 'the fall' also hints at the American autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: One who tots up figures adds them, and before a tumble a person staggers or wobbles.
